query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In lightweight HEAs, a homogeneous single‐phase microstructure composed of low-density elements (e.g. Al, Cr, Ti, V) promotes a synergistic effect—through pronounced lattice distortion and high mixing entropy—that enables the in situ formation of a thin, continuous, and self-healing oxide/passivation layer at high temperatures. However, minor additions of elements like Cu, which tend to segregate, disrupt this uniform oxide formation and introduce galvanic sites that compromise corrosion resistance and weaken mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase lightweight HEA (e.g. AlCrTiV0.5) with uniformly distributed elements.
generation.intervention: Prepare a series of alloys by intentionally varying the copper content (i.e. synthesizing AlCrTiV0.5Cux with incremental x values) under identical processing conditions.
generation.conditions: Test the alloys under high-temperature oxidation (e.g. air exposure at ~900°C) and in corrosive environments (e.g. electrochemical testing in 0.6 M NaCl), as well as under mechanical load (tensile/compression tests). The baseline for comparison is the Cu-free alloy that shows a continuous, dense protective oxide layer.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniform nanostructure of the Cu-free alloy enables formation of a protective oxide/passivation layer. Introduction of Cu leads to its segregation into Cu-rich phases (especially at grain boundaries), which interrupts oxide continuity and promotes micro-galvanic corrosion.
generation.mechanism: Lattice distortion arising from the random mixing of lightweight elements stabilizes both the microstructure and the protective oxide formation, underpinning high mechanical strength and corrosion/oxidation resistance. Conversely, Cu segregation creates heterogeneities that act as weak links during oxidation and corrosion, leading to increased current densities and reduced mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Cu-free or low-Cu HEA will maintain high yield strength with low corrosion current densities and minimal oxidation mass gain, whereas increasing Cu content will result in microstructural segregation, higher corrosion rates (e.g. elevated self-corrosion current densities), disrupted oxide scales, and diminished mechanical performance relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: A Cu-free AlCrTiV0.5 alloy that exhibits a uniform microstructure, continuous protective oxide layer, high corrosion resistance, and superior mechanical strength.
generation.boundary: When the alloy composition or processing conditions lead to significant phase segregation (e.g., when excessive Cu is added or when prolonged high-temperature exposure facilitates coarsening), the beneficial synergy between the high mixing entropy and protective oxide formation will be lost.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical Cu concentration and specific processing parameters at which segregation becomes detrimental are not rigorously defined and may vary with slight compositional or processing differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of AlCrTiV0.5Cux alloys with varying Cu concentrations under identical processing conditions. Characterize the alloys via microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) to detect any Cu-induced segregation, measure oxidation behavior (mass gain during high-temperature exposure at ~900°C), assess corrosion resistance (electrochemical impedance and potentiodynamic polarization in 0.6 M NaCl), and evaluate mechanical properties (tensile or compressive yield strength).
measurements: Microstructural analysis to determine elemental distribution and identification of Cu-rich segregated phases
Oxidation mass gain and oxide layer continuity via surface analysis
Corrosion current density and pitting potential from electrochemical tests
Mechanical performance metrics such as yield strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing Cu content does not lead to detectable segregation accompanied by a measurable degradation in oxidation resistance, corrosion resistance, or mechanical properties—instead showing similar or improved performance relative to the Cu-free baseline—the hypothesis that Cu-induced segregation disrupts the protective oxide layer would be falsified.

A Lightweight AlCrTiV0.5Cux High-Entropy Alloy with Excellent Corrosion Resistance

Abstract: Lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of low-density, high strength-to-weight ratio metallic structural material. Understanding their corrosion behavior is crucial for designing microstructures for their practical applications. This work investigates the electrochemical corrosion behavior of lightweight HEAs AlCrTiV0.5Cux (x = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0) in a 0.6 M NaCl solution. These HEAs were produced by vacuum arc melting. In contrast to 304L stainless steel, all of the alloys exhibited lower current density levels caused by self-corrosion, with AlCrTiV0.5 demonstrating the highest corrosion resistance (0.131 μA/cm2). Corrosion resistance decreased along with the content of copper because copper segregation accelerated local corrosion throughout the alloy.

Unraveling the Excellent High-Temperature Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCuAl-Based Alloy

Abstract: This study synthesized FeNiCuAlX high-entropy alloys (HEAs) (where X = Cr, Co, Mn) using arc melting and investigated their high-temperature oxidation behavior in air at 900 °C. The oxidation kinetics of all alloys followed a parabolic rate, with the oxidation rate constants (kp) of FeNiCuAlCr, FeNiCuAlCo, and FeNiCuAlMn being approximately two to three orders of magnitude lower than that of the FeNiCu alloy. Specifically, FeNiCuAlCr exhibited the lowest kp value of 1.72 × 10−6 mg2·cm4/s, which is significantly lower than those of FeNiCuAlCo (3.29 × 10−6 mg2·cm4/s) and FeNiCuAlMn (1.71 × 10−5 mg2·cm4/s). This suggests that the addition of chromium promotes the formation of a dense Al2O3/Cr2O3 oxide layer, significantly enhancing the oxidation resistance. Furthermore, corrosion resistance was assessed through potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy in a 3.5% NaCl solution. A Lightweight AlTiVNb High-Entropy Alloy Film with High Strength-Ductility Synergy and Corrosion Resistance

Abstract: The simultaneous improvement of mechanical and corrosion resistance is of great significance for engineering applications. In this work, a novel lightweight amorphous structure AlTiVNb high-entropy alloy (HEA) film was fabricated by magnetron sputtering. The compression test of the AlTiVNb HEA film nanopillar exhibits a high compressive strength of up to 3.6 GPa and deformability approaching 58%. The high strength is affected by the disordered state, the nanostructure, and the lattice distortion effect, while the high ductility comes from the ductile shear band and the island structure. In addition, the AlTiVNb HEA film shows a current density of 4.90 × 10−8 A/cm2 and a potential of −0.234 V in the 3.5% NaCl solution, comparable to that of the 316L stainless steel. The chemical disorder state, cocktail effect, and homogeneous amorphous structure contribute to excellent corrosion resistance. This finding offers new insights into high-performance HEA films with robust mechanical and anticorrosion performances for microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials.
